messages.subject: Few more DSM queries
parts:
Hi Guys,

First of all, thanks for the awesome tutorials online, and the slides to download, really helped me through the DSM process I've been following the helpful tips here for a while.

I've been creating DSM for 7 species of ungulate in a Savannah ecosystem, based on an extensive transect data set spanning several years. I've split this into seasonal classifications and I'm looking at the spatial abundance changes across three seasons (wet, dry, and drought). I've used a spatial smooth term s(x,y) for all models, and have investigated the effect of four variables (distance to water, distance to settlement, NDVI, NDVI - Seasonal variation)  Just a few questions:
  1. For some species in some seasons I have a very severe gradient across the study area often caused by management. For example, cattle in certain areas. This is mostly fine, but the fitted surface has increased unrealistically as predictions are made further from the survey effort. After reading around I have used Duchon splines over Thin plate splines for the s(x,y) term. This helped for most problematic sets, but not all, any thoughts on this? 
  2.  I've split the data into certain seasonal classifications and multiplied the amount of effort accordingly, but are there any other ways to look at the temporal trends. The surveys occurred monthly for nearly two years, and all variable data is available at a monthly scale. I saw briefly in some of the slides about tensors for space-time?
  3. I saw last weeks message about point counts, I'd be very interested in looking at how DSM can be applied to point counts, which we have a good database of collection for ungulates.
Thanks again in advance,

Peter Tyrrell
SORALO
www.soralo.org

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Few more DSM queries
parts:
Hi Peter, hi listfolk,

First off, very glad to hear that the materials are useful!

To your questions:

1. Duchon splines: do you mean that there are still "extreme"
predictions far from the data or that the estimated abundance over the
whole study area is still too high? The former should be what Duchon
splines guard against, but as we are still experimenting with them in
practice, it's possible there are still some behaviours we're not aware
of yet. In the latter case, this is still possible as we don't guarantee
that the remaining effects in the model are zero outside the data, just
that they are constant (and that constant could be big). If it is the
former case please do contact me offlist with an example, as I'd be very
interested in taking a look. Another possible basis that you may want to
try (if you haven't already) is "ts" (thin plate splines with shrinkage)
which may be useful.

2. Temporal trends: if you have sufficient coverage, it may be possible
to build a term like: te(x, y, time, d=c(2, 1), bs=c("ts", "cr")) or
somesuch which would give you a 2d spatial term interacting with time.
That being said there are some important caveats about using this kind
of model. Specifically ensuring that the coverage of your survey is
similar year-on-year seems sensible (you don't want to predict for 2010
using data from 2006 if there was some change in distribution between
those dates and you won't know if there was if there was no survey
effort). As with Duchon splines I think this lives in the "experimental"
side of things at the moment, so it's worth being cautious.

3. More on point counts soon. This is on my todo list at the moment.


Hope this helps!

best,
--dave
